name: Portfolio Optimisation Beyond Mean and Variance
title: Portfolio Optimisation Beyond Mean and Variance
answer: Portfolio optimisation beyond mean and variance moves away from Markowitz's two-moment model to account for skewness, kurtosis, tail risk, and non-normal return distributions. It covers objectives such as minimising conditional value at risk, controlling maximum drawdown, and targeting higher-moment preferences. The site tracks 117 listed AI-related instruments with daily prices, which provides a concrete universe for testing these approaches. This area sits within portfolio construction and draws on the AI Economist's coverage of AI-related equities, funds, and derivatives.

It covers objectives such as minimising conditional value at risk, controlling maximum drawdown, and targeting higher-moment preferences. sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on daily price series, corporate filings, and market data for the tracked AI-related instruments. Computation typically uses Python or R with optimisation libraries for nonlinear and nonconvex problems, and may require Monte Carlo simulation or historical resampling to estimate tail measures. Data pipelines need to handle missing prices, corporate actions, and survivorship bias in the AI instrument universe. Cloud or local compute is sufficient for most single-period and multi-period models, though scenario generation can be compute heavy.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Practitioners replace or augment the covariance matrix with measures of downside deviation, lower partial moments, or copula-based dependence. Common techniques include mean-CVaR optimisation, higher-moment portfolio selection with polynomial goal programming, and robust optimisation under estimation uncertainty. Machine learning enters through regime detection, clustering of return environments, or direct estimation of portfolio weights from features, but the core remains a constrained optimisation problem. Backtesting uses rolling windows and out-of-sample tests to check whether the added complexity improves realised risk-adjusted performance.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk questions centre on data provenance, model opacity, and the danger of overfitting to short AI-market history. A portfolio built on higher moments can concentrate in illiquid or volatile names, so risk limits and disclosure of tail assumptions matter. The site's 142 active AI lawsuits and 210 compliance and regulation pages are a reminder that AI-related instruments carry legal and regulatory exposure that a pure return distribution may miss. No part of this is investment advice; the work describes how such models are built and reviewed, not what any investor should hold.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward multi-period and goal-based optimisation that treats drawdown and path dependence as first-class constraints, not afterthoughts. As the AI instrument universe matures, expect more use of learned factor structures and uncertainty-aware optimisation that reports confidence intervals around weights. Integration with text and filing data may allow forward-looking tail scenarios rather than relying only on historical prices. The field is likely to converge on hybrid models that keep the interpretability of convex risk measures while borrowing from machine learning for regime and dependence estimation.
